MF
Web Designer — Graphic Designer — Digital Marketer

Design isn't
decoration.

I'm Malik Fawad — a web designer, graphic designer and digital marketer who builds brands that look considered and are built to perform, not just decorate a page.

As a web designer, I design and build responsive, motion-led sites and interfaces — from marketing pages to product dashboards — where load speed, clarity and usability matter as much as the visuals.

As a graphic designer, I develop identity systems, packaging and print/social collateral — logos, flyers, ads and greeting cards — built to hold up consistently across every format a brand actually gets used in.

On the marketing side, I plan and design the assets that carry a brand into the world — campaign creative, social templates and landing pages built around a clear funnel, not just a pretty layout.

My work spans brand identity, UI/UX and web design, with a technical background in AutoCAD that shapes how I think about structure, precision and systems long before a screen is involved.

Every project starts with the same question — what is this actually trying to do — and the design follows from the answer, not the other way around.

Questions,
answered.

Send a short brief through the contact form or book a call directly — either way, I'll follow up with a few questions before proposing scope and timeline.
Discover, strategize, design, refine, deliver — outlined above. Every project runs through all five stages, though the time spent in each depends on scope.
A focused brand identity typically runs 2–3 weeks; a full web or product design engagement is usually 4–8 weeks depending on scope and revisions.
Two structured rounds of revisions are built into every proposal. Additional rounds can be added if the scope changes mid-project.
Yes — most of my client work is remote, and I keep a flexible schedule to overlap with different time zones for calls.
Yes — the strategize stage of every project covers positioning and messaging direction before any visual design work begins.
